Distressed real estate is the model. There are just as many, if not more, wholesalers in lower-middle-class areas, middle-class areas, upper-middle-class areas, and upper-class areas. And yes, wholesalers must disclose what they are doing. But he also is concerned that many wholesalers transact incorrectly. He said there is a small percentage of wholesalers, in my opinion, that do the business correctly. Then the article quoted me. What is the AARP going to do? Force them to stay in their home or force them to pass it down to their kids? This gets even more ridiculous, Jones said. But one of the challenges is as our businesses grow, our ability to lead becomes just as important as our ability to do real estate deals. Can we achieve success in business while still being good spouses and parents and leaders that we want to be? And for more than four decades, he's taught leadership and personal growth to audiences around the world, from Fortune 500 companies to nonprofits and educational institutions. videos.title: The Real Cost of Running a Wholesale Business (My Actual Numbers)
videos.transcript: Everyone likes to talk about how much money you can make wholesaling a house, including me. But no one ever talks about how much it costs to operate a legit wholesale business and what your actual net profit is at the end of the month or year. In business, it's not what you make, it's what you keep. So, if you're a new wholesaler, by the end of this video, you're going to know exactly what expenses and net profit need to be so that you can build a sustainable business as you grow. And if you're an existing operator, you're going to learn the industry standards so that you can audit your own business and see where you need to make adjustments and improve. All that and more coming up. This video is brought to you by People Leads Pro, the new dispo feature for Propire that makes finding the right buyer for your deals faster than ever before. Instead of wasting time with stale cash buyer lists, People Leads Pro helps you find active buyers and gives you buy boxes and past transactions so you can see what they buy, where they buy, and when they buy. Find better buyers, build better relationships, and move your deals faster. Go to peopleleadspro.com now. Hurry, spots are going fast. Go to peopleleadspro.com to claim your spot. >> Hey, if you're new here, my name is Jerry Norton. I've been wholesaling and flipping real estate for over 21 years. And here on my YouTube channel, I show you how to master the process. So, if you want to be a flipping genius like me, subscribe to my channel and watch my videos. I just reviewed our P&Ls for last month in my Tulsa, Oklahoma wholesale operation with my business partner, Mark Gabriel. In September, we closed seven transactions for a total of $152,576 in gross revenue. Now, we track our metrics and financials meticulously so we can predict with a high level of certainty the number of deals, revenue, expenses, and net profit. Now, this year, we've been averaging around 10 to 11 deals a month. So, we're on track to do about 125 deals or so for the year. So, September was a lighter month with only seven closed deals, but it will serve well to illustrate how to understand and track the financials. At 152,000 in revenue over seven deals, that gave us an average of 21,700 revenue per deal. So, where did all that money go? Now, the first expense that we're going to discuss is advertising and marketing. For the month of September, we spent $39,899 in total marketing or approximately 25% of our revenue over seven deals. That comes to a $5,700 cost per deal. That means our return on ad spend or what's commonly referred to as rorowaz was 3.8. The way to understand rorowaz is for every dollar we spent in marketing to generate leads, we earned $3.8 in revenue. Now rorowaz is one of the most important financial metrics to track in business, especially a wholesale operation. If you're not getting at least 3x rorowaz, you cannot maintain a sustainable wholesale operation. Let me repeat that. If you are not hitting a 3x rorowaz, you cannot build a sustainable business. When it comes to your marketing budget, it should equal 25% of your revenue. That means as a general benchmark, if you earn a 100,000 in wholesale revenue, you should be spending 25,000 in marketing. Now, one of the mistakes I see wholesalers do when they start to struggle is they cut the marketing budget. That's the last expense to cut. I'll keep breaking down the financials, but first, let me tell you a quick story. I recently did a financial audit with a wholesaler in the Metro Detroit market who's been struggling with his wholesale business. After looking over his 2025 financials, I discovered that he did 45 deals for approximately $450,000 in annual revenue. That came to about $10,000 in revenue per deal. Now, what was alarming is his marketing cost was also $450,000 or $10,000 cost per deal. Now, do you see a problem? He's at break even without payroll, overhead, or anything else. Spent 10,000 in marketing to generate 10,000 in revenue is a quick and painful death. Now, fortunately, 2026 is looking much better, thank God. But in 2025, he was hemorrhaging cash. So, I told him two things have to happen. If you continue to spend 10,000 to acquire a customer, you have to increase revenue to 30,000 per deal. Or if you want to keep your average revenue per deal at 10,000, you have to lower your average marketing cost per deal to only 3,300. Remember, rorowaz has to be a minimum of 3x. Spend 10,000, earn 30,000 or earn 10,000, spend 3,300. You cannot sustain a profitable business unless you hit a minimum 3x rorowaz. Now, ideally, he does a combination of both. Lower his cost per deal to let's say 6,000 and increase his revenue per deal to at least 18,000. Listen, if I ever bump into you walking down the street and I ask you your rorowaz, if it's not 3x, I'm going to slap you. And by the way, if anyone ever claims a really high rorowaz, like a 10x, they either got lucky one time or they're lying. It doesn't exist. The reason is as you scale, you have to broaden your audience so that your cost per deal will creep up and you will probably do more deals. So your margin will go down. Now, I think our wholesale operation is probably more profitable than many other operators doing three times more deals. And that's why bigger isn't necessarily better. Now, our goal in Tulsa is to continue to grow revenue without compromising our desired net profit. I'll explain more as we go, so keep watching. The next biggest expense in a wholesale business is payroll. But before I move away from marketing, what I don't have time to talk about on this video is how to choose the right channels that will give you the desired 3x rorowaz. Lead genen is the lifeblood of any wholesale business, so you have to get it right. That's why I put together a marketing guide that outlines the top 10 marketing channels for wholesalers and how to decide which one is right for you. Not all leads are created equal, so you need to know the difference between inbound and outbound leads. This guide will help you identify your marketing sweet spot based on your budget, your goals, and your timeline. Best of all, I'll give you my marketing guide for free. Just comment below marketing guide and I'll give you the free download link. Okay, now let's talk about that next biggest expense to track in your wholesale operation. Payroll. Now, payroll is your team expense, including commission salespeople, contract labor, and your salary if you take a salary. Payroll should also be 25% of revenue. In our Tulsa operation, Mark and I don't take a payroll check. So, I'll explain how to compensate for that. Looking at our books in September, our payroll only came to $12,542. That was only 8% of revenue. But like I said, we don't take a monthly salary, but rather a distribution. Now, we believe you eat what you kill, and we like to leave as much cash as we can in the business as retained earnings. But if we did take a draw for September to keep payroll at 25% of revenue, there would be about $25,000 to go around. The third expense to track in a wholesale operation is general and administrative or GNA for short. This is basically your overhead to keep the lights on. Subscriptions, computers, office, cars, etc. GNA should not exceed 15% of revenue. Our GNA for September was 22,265 which is right at 15%. So, if your marketing is 25%, your payroll is 25%, and your GNA is 15%. That means what's left is 35% for profit and tax. In September, our profit was $74,710, which is right at 50%. But remember, that doesn't include payroll for me or Mark. Now, that, my friends, is what a healthy wholesale business should look like. And as we finish this year and head into next year, it's even more important than ever that you follow sound business principles so you build a predictable and sustainable wholesale business. So be sure to get my free marketing guide. Comment marketing guide below and I'll give you that free download. So let's take a minute now and discuss how to read your P&L. You start with gross revenue minus cost of goods sold or COGS and that equals your net operating income or NOI. Let's talk about COGS. Cogs is anything required to create the revenue. In a true wholesale operation, we don't really have COGS because we're not buying or renovating the properties. However, in a flipping business, your purchase and rehab would be COGS. For example, let's say you bought a rehab for 200,000, spent $100,000 on the rehab, and then sold it for 400,000. In that example, you would take the revenue of 400,000 minus the purchase of 200,000 minus the rehab of a 100,000 to get a net operating income of 100,000. The purchase and the rehab is a cost of goods sold, COGS, because we can't generate the 400,000 sale without it. Does that make sense? By the way, why is marketing not a COGS? Because you spend the money with no guarantee of a sale. Now, are you clear on COGS? So, you have gross revenue minus COGS equals net operating income. From there, you subtract your marketing of 25% of NOI, payroll at 25%, GNA at 15% to get a remaining 35% for profit and tax. Now, here's the bottom line. Being a successful wholesaler is not just about sellers, cash buyers, and contracts. You also need to understand and follow sound business and financial principles. I highly recommend you hire a bookkeeper and you review your financials at least monthly. Now, I like to review mine every week. When I first started 20 years ago, I had a bookkeeper that came to my home office every Friday for a few hours to reconcile my accounts and give me reports and most importantly review cash flow and make cash flow projections. Today, the goal of our wholesale operation and my other businesses is to build an operation that is reliable, predictable, and sustainable. And the only way that's possible is to understand exactly how your sales process works and then execute relentlessly. And the way to know if it's working effectively is to measure and track each step in the sales process. So download my marketing guide, comment marketing guide in the comments below for the link. And be sure to watch this next video where I'm going to show you the five most important metrics to measure and track and give you the best practices for your business so that you know what to strive for. videos.transcript: One of the most overlooked ways to find real estate deals is sitting right in front of you, >> [music] >> real estate agents. And I'm not talking about waiting for an agent to randomly send you a deal. I'm talking about intentionally reaching out to agents, building relationships with them, and getting them to bring you off-market properties not yet listed for sale. I'm talking about properties where the seller is actually motivated to sell at a discount for all cash. We call this agent outreach, and most wholesalers screw this up because they don't follow a proven and sales process. So, in this video, I'm going to give you the playbook and walk you through the exact framework that we use with agent outreach, and I'm even going to show you how to get instant access to every agent in your market. So, if you're serious about wholesaling with agents, this is a video you don't want to miss. Coming up. >> This video is brought to you by People Leads Pro, the easiest way to find the right buyer for your real estate deals. With People Leads Pro, you get 10 million cash buyers across the country, including active [music] flippers, active cash buyers, active land buyers, and active landlords. Plus, you can see buy boxes and past transactions, so you know exactly what they want to buy. Stop guessing who to contact. Find the right buyer for your deal with People Leads Pro. Go to peopleleadspro.com to get started. >> If you're new here, my name is Jerry Norton. I've been wholesaling and flipping real estate for over 21 years, and here on my YouTube channel, I show you how to master the process. So, if you want to be a flipping genius like me and live your dream life, subscribe to my channel and watch my videos. If done correctly, agent outreach is a powerful strategy to get agents to bird dog off-market properties for you. Remember, agents go on listing appointments every single day, and some of those sellers have a property in poor condition and are motivated to sell at a discount. It could be a property that is inherited, vacant, an unwanted rental, or even just a seller who wants to move quickly or doesn't want to go through the normal retail process of listing their property on market. Those properties can be phenomenal wholesale opportunities, and here's the other thing you need to remember. The agent wants to get paid. So, instead of treating the agent like an obstacle between you and the seller, the goal is to make the agent your ally. If there's a way for the agent to represent the seller and participate on the buyer side as well, that's a huge benefit to the agent, especially if the agent never has to list it on the open market. Now, everybody has a reason to get the deal done. Your goal as a wholesaler is to train agents to bring those distressed seller leads to you. And after transacting millions in revenue with agents, we've perfected the process. So, let me walk you through how this process actually happens. I follow a two-call framework. I'm going to give you the questions to ask on the first call, show you how to present your numbers on the second call, and I'll even show you how to respond when the agent thinks your ARV is too low or your rehab number is too high. Now, it's very important you watch this video to the end because I'm going to show you also the best place and the fastest method to find agents in any market in the US. So, keep watching. Let's start with call number one. The purpose of the first call is not to negotiate the deal. It's to do discovery. You're trying to understand four things. One, what's going on with the seller? Two, what's going on with the house? Three, what's the seller's timeline? And four, what's the seller expecting on price? That's it. Don't overcomplicate this. Let's walk through these steps. Step one is to find out if the agent has a lead. When the agent answers the phone, here's your intro. Hi Sarah, how are you doing? Awesome. I'm contacting you because me and my partners are looking to buy another investment property in the area. Is this something you can help me with? Great. We're looking for properties that are in original condition or need a lot of work and the seller is looking for a fast and convenient cash offer. And lately it's been difficult to find any properties on the MLS that makes sense. Do you have any properties with motivated sellers coming up or do you know if any agents in your office know of any properties that need work and are about to hit the market? Now if the agent says no, respond by saying, "No worries. I'm going to send you my contact information after we hang up so you can save it in your phone. If any distressed properties come up in the future, will you call me? By the way, I would love to have you write the offers for us. This way you can keep both sides of the commission on all your listings." Now if the agent says they do have a property coming up, then you want to ask five important discovery questions. The first question is obvious, what is the property address? But be ready for some agents to be reluctant to tell you. Agents will sometimes protect the address because they don't yet have a formal listing agreement with the seller or maybe because the seller requested privacy or maybe they don't yet trust you. Now if that happens, simply say, "Hey, I totally understand. If you'd like, you can send me a property specific buyer agreement. I'd be happy to sign that. I'm not trying to go around you and if we end up buying the property, I'd want you involved in the transaction." Now that reassurance is important. Your goal is to make the agent [clears throat] feel safe working with you. Now once you have the address, next is to find out the seller situation. A great way to ask this is to say, "Can you catch me up to speed on what's going on with the seller?" Or an even more casual way to ask it, "What's the story on this house?" You're looking for the agent to reveal the seller's motivation. Sometimes the agent will tell you everything you need to know. They inherited the house, the tenant just moved out, the seller relocated and the house has been vacant for 6 months, they started fixing it up and ran out of money or they need to close quickly. Sometimes the agent won't tell you too much, so you need to ask more specific questions such as, was this owner-occupied or was it a rental? Is anybody living there right now? How long has it been vacant? Those questions keep the conversation flowing naturally and get the agent to share more details. Now, another way to uncover motivation is to ask, what made the seller decide to sell? That's a very natural question to ask. Remember, the better you understand the seller's problem, the better you'll know if you can actually solve the problem. Next, you want to get a basic understanding on the condition of the property. Get a general sense by asking, what kind of condition is the house in? Or, what repairs do you think it needs? Now, if the agent says the seller lived there for 30 years and hasn't updated anything, then you know it's probably a complete rehab. If they say the house was remodeled 5 years ago, then it might be in decent condition. Now, you could ask about big ticket items. Any idea how old the roof is? Or, how about the HVAC? What you're trying to determine is whether this is a light, average, or heavy renovation. Finally, the fourth question is to understand the timeline and if there is urgency. Ask, how quickly are they looking to sell? Let's say the agent says they'd really like to get this done as soon as possible. Then say something like, we can typically close in 21 to 30 days. Would that work for them? If they say yes, then you know speed is important, making a cash offer more attractive. Finally, we need to know what price the seller wants. You can ask this a few different ways. What price point is the seller looking for? Or, how much would the seller like to get for the house? Now, don't be afraid to ask. You're trying to determine whether you and the seller are even remotely in the same universe. But, don't let the seller's asking price deter you from moving forward. Often times, the seller's asking price and their acceptance price are two different things. Now, after following the five discovery questions, step two is to get pictures from the agent. You need pictures to properly evaluate the condition, and if you get the deal, you're going to need them later when you market the property to a cash buyer. Ask the agent, "Do you have any pictures yet?" If they do, great. Tell them to send you whatever pictures and videos they have right on their phone. Now, if they don't, then ask, "Would you be able to get some pictures and video for me? When do you think you could get those?" Now, at this point, there are a few important things to consider. First, how do you handle if the property is already listed for sale by the agent? Now, if that's the case, then say, "I noticed this property is already up for sale. What kind of feedback have you gotten from buyers so far?" That's an incredibly valuable question. Maybe buyers keep saying it needs too much work. Maybe financing is difficult. Maybe the floor plan is weird. Maybe everybody thinks it's overpriced. If it is overpriced, I'll say, "Since this is going to be a flip and needs to be renovated, I probably can't get anywhere close to the asking price. Just so I don't waste your time, what kind of offers have you already turned down?" Now, that will give you some visibility on where the seller is at. However, motivation changes monthly, weekly, and sometimes daily, so I typically will still make my offer even if it's lower than other offers previously rejected. Now, the third step on call number one is to ensure the agent understands how they make money working with you and why it's beneficial. Say something like this. "Just to be clear with you, I'm unrepresented, and I'd like you to represent me on the buyer side. Now, there are a few different ways we can handle your commission. You could dual represent and get a commission from both the seller and from me as the buyer, or I could cover the entire commission. That way, the seller doesn't have to worry about paying you. Either way, I want to make sure you get paid well for working with me. Which way do you prefer?" The goal is to get agents double commission so they are excited to make a deal happen and work with you in the future. The last step on call one is to set up the agent for our offer which happens on call two. Say to the agent, "Let me run some numbers with my partners. We're going to look at comps and we're going to estimate the renovation budget and then I'll get back to you right away." Now, I like to wait for a few reasons. One, the agent respects more that I'm going to crunch numbers rather than offer right there on the spot. And two, it gives me a chance to do proper due diligence and even possibly pre-sell to my buyers. Okay, that leads into call number two. During call two, the key is not just to make your offer, it's to get the agent to understand how you arrived at your number. Remember, the offer has to logically make sense to the agent because if they have to go back to the seller and sell them on why they should accept your offer. So, step one on call two is to start with the after repair value or ARV. Sarah, we ran the numbers on 123 Main Street and I want to go over a couple of things with you. We're planning to renovate and resell this one. What do you think the resale value would be assuming we fix it up to top market standards? Now, this question is strategic. You want the agent involved in the underwriting conversation. Let's say they respond with, "I think it's sell for 400,000." Compare that to your comps. If your number is reasonably close, great. We're starting from common ground. If their ARV is much higher, don't tell them they're wrong. Ask them, "We're seeing something a little different. Which comps are you using?" It's important to shift from opinions to data. Be open and curious because they may have a comp or information you missed. Once you're clear on the ARV, step two is to ask about the rehab cost. "If we completely renovate this house inside and out, what do you think the rehab budget would be?" Now, this is where agents and investors often see things differently. Most agents underestimate the cost to renovate. The agent may say, "I think you could fix it up for 30,000." Now, when that happens, explain what actually needs done. My partners are not just painting it and putting it back on the market. They're going to maximize the resale. We're probably doing flooring, paint, kitchen, bathrooms, fixtures, landscaping, and we may have HVAC, roof, or other major items. Now, the rehab number begins to make sense. After getting clear on ARV and the rehab, it's time to walk the agent through your math. Like I said, most agents are logical in nature, so it's important they understand how you arrived at your offer. So, say something like, "Let me show you how we got to our number. We're estimating the resale value at approximately 400,000. Then we've got roughly 60,000 in renovation. On top of that, we've got commissions when we resell it, closing costs, financing costs, interest, utilities, insurance, and other carrying costs. videos.title: You’ll Keep Losing Wholesale Deals Until You Learn to Close Sellers
videos.transcript: Most wholesalers lose the deal before they ever make an offer. They ask the seller what price they want, immediately start negotiating against that price, only to discover the seller was never prepared to sell their house in the first place. On this video, I'm going to show you a different way to negotiate with motivated [music] sellers. You're going to learn how to get a seller's commitment before negotiating price, [music] how to uncover their real bottom line, and how to negotiate without sounding aggressive, [music] manipulative, or desperate. And best of all, I'm going to give you the exact questions that you need to use [music] on your next seller call. All that and more coming up. >> For a limited time, you [music] can get a free copy of Jerry Norton's motivated seller scripts so you can talk to, email, and text sellers with [music] confidence. Download it now at freeellerscripts.com. >> If you're new here, my name is Jerry Norton. I've been wholesaling and flipping real estate for over 21 years. And after all these years talking to sellers, I think the biggest mistake most inexperienced wholesalers make is they believe closing a seller means convincing him to accept their offer. That is not your job. Your job is to understand the seller's situation, determine whether you can actually solve their problem, and then help the seller reach a decision. Sometimes that decision will be to do business with you, and sometimes it won't. When you're willing to walk away from deals that don't work, it takes the pressure off of you. And it also takes the pressure off of the seller. And when sellers feel like they're being pressured, they become defensive. When they feel understood and in control, they are more open. They trust you more. And they're much more willing to collaborate. Never forget, distressed sellers often care more about certainty than price. So before you start negotiating price, slow down and focus on understanding the seller situation first. Use a technique called labeling. Labeling is when you repeat back what the seller appears to be thinking or feeling. One way to help you do this is by using it sounds like or it seems like phrases. You could say it sounds like you've been dealing with this property for quite a while. Or it seems like getting this handled without making repairs is important to you. or it sounds like you're concerned that an investor might agree to one price and then try to renegotiate later. Notice that you're not assuming you know or you're not arguing with the seller or defending yourself. Even if you don't agree, you're simply labeling what the seller appears to be thinking or feeling. Then stop talking. Give them the opportunity to confirm it, correct it, or tell you more. Labeling helps you uncover the real reason they're considering selling. Another way to understand the seller's situation is to use a technique called mirroring. Mirroring is when you repeat the last one to three important words the seller said with an upward inflection like a question. For example, if you ask, "What price are you hoping to get for the property?" And the seller responds, "I'd like to get 250,000." A mirror would be 250,000. Then be quiet. Mirroring encourages the seller to share more. He may expand by saying, "Well, that's what Zillow says it's worth." Or, "Well, that's what I paid when I bought it in 2017." Mirroring helps the seller feel safe to share more, such as how he came up with his asking price. If the seller said, "Well, that's what Zillow says it's worth." You could respond by labeling, "It sounds like Zillow's estimate is playing a big role in how you're valuing the property." Then let the seller confirm, correct, or share more. Remember, the point of labeling and mirroring is to help the seller feel seen and heard. So, in turn, he opens up and is more collaborative with you when it comes time to negotiate a deal. Like I said, be careful you don't assume you know what the seller is experiencing. Once you think you've got it, summarize the seller's situation back to him. Say to him, "Let me make sure I understand what's going on. You inherited the property. It's been vacant for 6 months, and you don't want to put any money into it. Your biggest priorities are selling it as is, not paying commissions, and closing before the end of the month. Have I got that right? Now, you want the seller to say, "That's right." Because that's right means they believe you understand them. By the way, that process of making the seller feel safe happens from hello to goodbye. I call it BRT, building a relationship of trust, and it needs to happen through the entire sales process. Now, once you understand the seller situation and you've built a certain level of trust, the next step is to get a commitment from the seller to work with you before negotiating price. Now, I call this the pre-close, and it's one of the most important lessons in this entire video. Write this down. Never spend time negotiating price with someone who isn't willing and able to move forward right now. The idea here is small commitments lead to big commitments. A small commitment to work with you leads to a big commitment to sign a contract with you. Now, the best way to pre-close is by asking what's called nooriented questions. Let me explain what a nooriented question is. Instead of trying to force the seller to say yes, you frame the question so the seller can comfortably say no. For example, instead of asking, "Are you prepared to sign a contract?" I might ask, if we can agree on price and terms that work for both of us, would you be opposed to putting together an agreement today? Now, the correct answer is no. I wouldn't be opposed to that. No, wouldn't be opposed. That means yes, I'm willing to commit. Saying no can help the seller feel safer and move in control, while yesoriented questions can make them wonder what they're being pushed into. But don't stop after asking it once. I like to double tap the commitment. So, if I say, "If we can agree on price and terms, would you be opposed to putting together an agreement today?" And the seller says, "No, I wouldn't be opposed." Then solidify the seller is serious about committing. Ask it again. So, you wouldn't be opposed to putting pen to paper today if we can find something that works for both of us. Now, the reason it's important to ask twice is because the first response could just be a casual agreement. The second question asks the seller to consciously confirm that they are prepared to take action. Keep in mind, you're not getting a commitment to accept your price. You're getting a commitment to make a decision only if you can both reach acceptable terms. That distinction is very important. Once the seller commits to move forward, another important aspect of the pre-close is to verify the seller can actually make the decision to sell. Don't ask, "Are you the only decision maker?" because that can sound threatening. A better way to ask instead is, "Who else would be affected by the sale of this property?" Or another way I like to frame this question is, is there anyone who would be upset if we put a deal together today? Asking it this way gives them room to mention a spouse, a sibling, a business partner, etc. If they say, "I need to discuss it with my wife," you could respond by labeling. It sounds like making this decision together is important. Then ask, "What's the best way for us to include her in the conversation so that everyone has the same information? Is she available now?" Now, whenever possible, get everyone involved before negotiating price. Otherwise, you could negotiate the entire deal and then have to negotiate all over again with someone else. Hey, listen. I know I'm covering a lot of material in this video and it may seem a little overwhelming, but don't worry. I put together a detailed guide which outlines my entire sales process, all the steps, the scripts, what to say, how to overcome objections, and I call it my closer framework. And I'll give it to you for free. Stay to the end of this video to learn how. Okay. So, after the pre-close, finally, it's time to start the negotiation process. Now, before presenting an offer, first get the seller to negotiate against himself. Let me demonstrate how this might look. Let's say the seller's initial asking price was 250,000. At this point in the sales process, I might say something like, "For an ASIS allcash offer with no commissions or cost to you, where we close on your timeline, what would you be willing to take for an offer like that?" Now, by framing it this way, you're essentially soliciting a better price by highlighting the value you're bringing. Now, deliver it calmly and curiously than stop talking. You are giving the seller an opportunity to adjust their own number before you make an offer. They might say, "Well, I might be able to do 235." Now, they just came down 15,000 and you haven't even made an offer yet. Now, you could mirror them 235 where they might say, "Maybe 230,000, but I really couldn't go below that." Then you could respond, "I appreciate you trying to work with me. Is 230,000 the best you can do?" Then you silence again. Most people become uncomfortable with silence and they begin negotiating against themselves. So, don't rescue them by talking. Now, at this point, what do you do if the seller's adjusted price still doesn't work? Let's say the seller comes down to 230,000, but your maximum allowable offer is only 180,000. Start by acknowledging their effort and then ask a very important calibrated question. I call this the how am I supposed to do that question. So, it might sound like this. I appreciate you making an effort to work with me. Let me ask you a question. How do I make this work at 230,000 when the property needs significant work done and renovated properties are only selling for around 275,000 in that neighborhood? When you ask a how am I supposed to do that question, it invites the seller to confront the practical problem you're presenting and help find a solution. The seller might say, "Well, what could you pay?" Which opens the door for you to negotiate a better price. Okay, so after getting the seller to negotiate against himself, now it's time to negotiate the price. The goal is to start low and come up to a price that is satisfactory for both parties. You starting low and coming up is better than the seller starting high and coming down. The idea is that the seller walks away feeling like he worked you up rather than feeling like you worked him down. See the difference? That's why the initial low offer is what we call the anchor price. The anchor price needs to be a ballpark price and it needs to solicit a no. So, how do you do the low anchor? I usually anchor by saying one of two things. I'll say, "In a perfect world, it would be great to be in the low 100s." Another way I like to say it is, I imagine if you got other offers from investors like me, they would be in the high 200s. Now, this is very important. After giving the anchor, shut up. Resist the urge to talk. Let the silence negotiate for you. Don't talk and wait for the seller to respond. Remember, the anchor is a strategic rejection. So, the response should be, "There's no way I could go that low." If they don't say that, you probably didn't anchor low enough. When the seller rejects your anchor price, respond by saying, "Hey, I totally get it. That would be my price in a perfect world. But how close to that price can you get?" And this is where the seller will start to come down on price. Now, after the anchor is rejected, it's time to start the counter process or what I call closing the gap. The goal of closing the gap is to strategically counter back and forth by staying as close to the anchor as you can, but not to exceed the maximum allowable offer. The way this looks is you're going to anchor again slightly up from your initial anchor. So, if your anchor was in the low 100s and your MAO is, let's say, 150,000, you might say, "If I could get closer to the 115 range, how would that sound?" Followed by, "But how close to that can you get?" and continue to repeat the process, slowly coming up, closing the gap. Now, think about it this way. Every thousand dollars I can be under my MAO is another thousand dollar in profit I just made on the deal. So, once you've closed the gap and you're in the profit zone, finally give a firm offer. Say something like, "Hey, I really appreciate you working with me. I would love to put a deal together with you. If you would be willing to put together an agreement today, I would be willing to come up to 138,000. Can we make that happen? And at that point, lock up the deal and get it in writing. Now, I highly recommend you use my nationwide wholesale compliant contracts. I'll give them to you for free. Just go to wholesaler contracts.com for the free download. And like I promised, I'll give you my exact closer framework so that you have it as a blueprint. Use it to follow the steps and the sequences, learn the questions and the proper framing and how to overcome objections. Just go to mycloserframework.com to download it for free. Now, I created this framework as a result of talking to over 10,000 sellers and doing thousands of deals over the past 21 years. The key is practicing and learning how to overcome objections because the more comfortable you are following my closer framework, the easier and faster you'll do deals. So download that now. Go to mycloserframework.com. Now, on this video, I talked about how to close a seller. Once you do and you get an executed agreement, the next step in the wholesale process is to find a cash buyer for your deal. So, look no further. I have systems and capital in place to flip houses in pretty much any market. And I'm looking for more deals. So, I want to invite you to learn about a finder program where I'll pay you $10,000 for every deal you bring me that meets my criteria. videos.transcript: Did you know that you can wholesale on-market properties that are listed for sale with real estate agents? I've done it hundreds of times, but there are some challenges that can make it more difficult than wholesaling off-market properties. So, in this video, get ready to learn the six biggest challenges wholesaling on-market deals and how to overcome them, coming up. If you're new here, my name is Jerry Norton. I've been wholesaling and flipping real estate for over 21 years, and here on my YouTube channel, I show you how to master the process. So, if you want to be a flipping genius like me, subscribe to my channel and watch my videos. In case you don't know, on-market is when a seller hires a real estate agent to list and sell their property. When a property goes on-market, it becomes public and it shows up on Zillow, Redfin, Trulia, and realtor.com for everyone to see. This gets the seller maximum exposure and ideally the highest price the market is willing to pay. In return, the seller agrees to pay commissions on the gross sale price, which is typically 2 and 1/2% for the listing agent and 2 and 1/2% for the buyer's agent for a total of 5 to 6%. Now, the thing is most people, including a lot of real estate investors, think that only unmotivated retail sellers go on-market and you can't find distressed, discounted properties, or motivated sellers on-market, which is just not true. Some sellers look for a cash buyer off-market, and some sellers look for a cash buyer on-market. The reality is every day distressed, motivated sellers list properties for sale with agents, which means that you and me can find these deals, make offers, and get contracts. So, if you're a wholesaler, I want to make something very clear to you. Just because there is an agent representing the seller doesn't change the fundamentals of wholesaling. A contract with a seller is a contract with a seller. It doesn't matter if you're dealing directly with the seller, or an agent is helping the seller, a lawyer is helping the seller, or Donald Trump is helping the seller. Once you have an executed contract with a seller, you now have an equitable interest in the property. That contract is yours to do with as you please. You can perform on the contract and buy the property, or you can assign it to someone else. That's your right. Now, small caveat. There are wholesale laws and regulations, and depending on the state where you're transacting, there could be disclosure requirements, seller right to cancel requirements, licensing requirements, or contract restrictions that impact if and how you wholesale. Now, I cover regulation in detail here on my channel. I also maintain a free report which outlines the regulations in each state. To get that free report, just go to wholesaleregulations.com. So, from here on out, everything I'm going to share is contingent on the rules and laws in your state. So, if you're going to wholesale, it's your responsibility to know, understand, and follow the laws and rules in your state. But, going back to listed properties, the agent's job is to help the seller get an executed contract and see the deal to the closing. That's it. If you decide to assign your contract to someone else, that's on you to find a cash buyer and execute an assignment contract and notify title. It does not involve the agent, and technically, there is nothing the agent can do about it. They may not like it, but at closing, the seller gets exactly what is stated in the contract, and the agent gets their exact commission, same as if you bought the property yourself. Now, having said that, I realize there are some challenges with wholesaling on market properties that are unique that you don't have to deal with when wholesaling off market. So, let's go over the six biggest challenges and how to overcome them. But, first, I want to point out something that I can't iterate enough. And that is that on market lead gen is free. It doesn't cost you anything to find on market deals. That's huge, especially if you don't have a marketing budget. In fact, if you have zero money for marketing, and you want to learn step-by-step how to get your first deal, be sure to check out the video where I break it down in detail. I'll put the link to that video in the description below. Okay, let's cover the six biggest challenges and how to overcome them. Challenge number one is dealing with a difficult agent. Maybe they don't like wholesalers, which is common. Yes, it's true that some agents can make the wholesaling process way more complicated than it needs to be. But just because you have a negative experience with a difficult agent, doesn't mean it doesn't work. Do you know how many complicated, uncooperative, hard to work with, difficult private sellers I've dealt with? Yeah, like most of them. Handle a difficult agent the same way you deal with a difficult private seller, or a difficult lender, or a difficult contractor, or a difficult teenager, or a difficult anybody. Work through the issues as best you can. Now, in the past, I typically wouldn't tell agents that I planned on wholesaling the property. First of all, it's none of their business what I do with the contract. And two, why create unnecessary drama? They would find out eventually at closing, and when they would, I would simply say, "I've got a lot going on right now, so I'm passing this deal on to one of my partners." Partner is referring to your cash buyer. I had an agent get upset one time when they found out at closing that I was wholesaling the deal, and I said to her, "I performed on the contract. We closed on time. The seller got exactly what we agreed in the contract, and you got paid your full commission. What's the problem?" But due to the high regulation environment that we're in, in recent years I've changed that position. I believe it's much better to fully disclose your intent upfront to that agent. I'd rather tell them at the time I'm contracting, or after the contract, but before starting the dispo process. Now, I put together very specific agent scripts that describe how to disclose to agents and overcome these objections. Stay till the end of this video, and I'll tell you how to get that for free. The second challenge wholesaling on-market properties is making sure your contract is assignable. Since the property is on market and there is an agent involved, they will use their state-approved contracts, but you have to make sure that the agent includes the right terms and clauses in the contract so that you can wholesale it. In fact, I created a 10-point offer sheet to provide the agents, which covers all of the essential elements of what needs included in the contract. Now, you simply provide that to the agent so they can make sure everything is included when they write the offer. That's also included with my free agent scripts, so stick around and I'll tell you how to get that for free. But, one of the most important things to make sure is that your contract can be assigned. Now, general rule of thumb is a contract by nature is assignable unless it states in writing that it cannot be assigned. This is called a no assignment clause, which means you would have to do a double closing wholesale and secure what's called transactional funding. Now, this is something my company provides. If you do need double closing funds, go to usejerryscash.com. We even do the first one for free, so check that out. Go to usejerryscash.com to learn more. So, remember, if the contract does not have a no assignment clause, then by default, you can assign it. But, if you want to be extra safe, where you put your name on the contract as the buyer, add the phrase and or assigns, which means you're the buyer or anyone you assign it to. So, if I sign the contract as the buyer using my LLC, Jerry Is a Flipping Genius LLC, I could add {comma} and or assigns, giving me the ability to later assign the contract to a cash buyer. If the contract does have a no assignment clause, such as bank-owned properties, then be sure to follow my workaround strategy using a designated LLC. This technique allows you to do a single closing wholesale, and I did a video that explains it in detail, including all of the paperwork you need. I'll put the link in the description below for you. The third challenge with wholesaling on-market properties is most agents require proof of funds and earnest money, which neither of those things usually come up with private sellers. Let's discuss each one. As a wholesaler, when you make a cash offer, most agents will call you out on that and basically say, "Prove that you have the cash." Now, if you have hundreds of thousands of dollars lying around like me, just show them a recent bank statement and all is good. But, if you don't have liquid cash sitting in a bank account in the amount of your offer, then you can provide a proof of funds letter, which basically says you have a financial relationship with a funding source who can provide you the funds assuming the deal meets certain requirements. A proof of funds letter is equivalent to a pre-approval letter from a lender, and in my experience, this is sufficient for about 90% of agents. And if you're a pro or prime-level subscriber to my wholesaling and house-flipping deal management system, Flipster, you get unlimited custom proof of funds letters for as many offers as you want. But, what do you do if the agent doesn't like the letter and wants to see hard proof of funds? Here's how to handle that. Tell the agent the following. "My partners and investors I work with can provide a hard proof of funds in the form of a bank statement, just like you want, but I can't ask them for that unless I first have a fully executed contract on the property. So, let's do this. Let's add a contingency clause to the contract that I will provide a hard proof of funds within 10 days of accepted offer." Now, earnest money is also expected with on-market properties. Earnest money is a good-faith deposit held in escrow at the title company and applied towards the purchase and is typically $500 to $1,000, but it could be as high as 10% of the offer price. Now, earnest money is not due until you get an accepted contract. And if you wholesale the deal, you'll get it reimbursed to you on the day of closing. But, I have a lot of people tell me, "Jerry, I don't have a thousand dollars for earnest money." My first response to that is, unlike off-market, which most methods cost thousands of dollars in marketing just to generate leads, finding on-market deals does not cost you anything for marketing. I typically spend three to five thousand dollars in marketing cost per off-market contract. I don't spend a dime with on-market. So, coming up with $500 or $1,000 to float earnest money for a few weeks until I get it back at closing is nothing compared to what you have to spend with off-market. Now, having said that, if earnest money is really an issue, here's a strategy similar to how to handle the proof of funds issue. Put in your contract that you need five or a 10-day inspection contingency for due diligence, and that the earnest money is due at the end of the inspection. Then, find your cash buyer and get him to provide the earnest money. Okay, the fourth challenge wholesaling on-market properties with agents is getting cash buyers access to the property because typically the agent needs to coordinate access with the seller, and in some cases, the agent wants to be present for the showing. So, you can see how that would complicate things with cash buyers. To overcome this, I make sure to address this issue up front. I get the agent to include in the contract in writing at the time of making my offer the following: Buyer to have unrestricted access to the property. Then, only show the property one time to all of your cash buyers. I call this an inspection party, and I did a video that breaks it down in detail, link in the description below. The fifth challenge wholesaling on-market properties is some cash buyers don't like to buy on-market properties. When you take your deal to a cash buyer and he googles the address, he'll see that it's on-market. He won't know your contract price, but he'll see that there's a list price and in some cases, regardless of the numbers or how good of a deal it is, if the wholesale price is anywhere near the list price, the cash buyer might feel like he's not getting a deal. For example, let's say that a property comes out for sale priced really aggressively for 175,000. And let's say that 175,000 is a great price for a flipper. And let's say that if you found the exact same deal off market, your cash buyer would buy it all day long for 175,000. But it's not off market, it's on market, which means nothing other than an agent is involved and it's public. And let's say that you get the contract for 160,000 and you take it to that cash buyer for 175,000. Even though 175,000 is a good deal and it fits his formula, he won't buy it because he feels like it's not a deal because he's paying list price. You see how that's a problem? Let me illustrate using a scenario that happened to me once. I got an awesome on market deal in Philadelphia that came out for sale at 100,000. Then he called me back a few hours later and he said he found out that it's on market and listed for 100,000 and now he no longer wants the deal. I said to him, "Why does that matter? If 125 is a deal for you, what does it matter if it's listed on market?" He said, "Because I could have bought it for 100,000. I'm overpaying at 125,000." I said, "But you didn't. I did. Stop counting the money in my pocket and count the money in your own pocket." So, I'll sell it to someone else for 125,000 who didn't care it was listed. But here's the reality, some cash buyers won't care about list price as long as the price fits their formula. Some won't be interested at all just because it's on market and some will be interested only if it's significantly lower than the list price. That way they feel like it's a deal. For example, I just got an on-market deal for 67,000 that was listed for 100,000. Now, I can wholesale that deal all day for 80,000 without much issue because the cash buyer price of 80,000 is significantly lower than the list price of 100,000. So, the cash buyer still feels like he's getting a deal. So, here's what I suggest. Go to your cash buyer who you have a relationship with or find a cash buyer that you can build a relationship with. Tell them that you want to go hard after on-market properties and make a lot of low offers. And tell them the following. If I find an on-market deal and I negotiate a great contract and I bring it to you at your exact buy formula and desired buy price, will you have an issue if it's on market? Now, this is very motivating for most agents. Now, some states don't allow dual agency. Now, if that's you, you can still accomplish the same objective by doing designated agency, which is using another agent to represent you in the same brokerage as the listing agent, or the list agent could become what's called a transaction broker, which means they don't represent the seller or the buyer in the transaction and still get both sides of the commission. videos.title: I Found The Worst Real Estate Agent (how to avoid bad agents)
videos.transcript: I think I just found the worst real estate agent in East Tennessee. This guy, Nick Dimitropoulos with Greater Impact Realty. In this video, I'm going to share with you what happened. And if you're a buyer in the market, whether you're a retail buyer or an investor, I want to share with you what to watch out for with buyer's agents like this. So, about 6 months ago, my son Jared decided to move to East Tennessee with his wife Britta. At the time, they were managing my hotel. So, they started to look around and started to get a feel for the market and what kind of house they wanted, where, how close to us, and just normal first-time home buyer type of research. And at the time, I said to Jared, I said, "Jared, make sure before you start going and looking at houses that you get pre-approved with a lender, so you know, you know, what you can afford, what kind of down payment, what kind of interest rate, just so you can go out and look at houses and know what you can get." But this was early on, they did not do that. They were just coming and visiting for a few days in town, and they wanted to go look at some properties. So, they found this house on Zillow that they thought was interesting. And on the Zillow, they saw the contact agent, you know, button next to the listing, which is very deceiving for Zillow, because a lot of people think that that's the agent for the property. And so, Jared and Britta clicked on that, and they contacted this Nick guy, who it was just an ad, he was not the listing agent for the property, but he agreed to show them this property. Now, again, they were not pre-approved. First-time home buyer not pre-approved. So, first sign of a terrible agent is you show a first-time home buyer property without a pre-approval, because there's a high likelihood that you're wasting your time with someone who can't even buy a house. But he decided to anyway. And not only did he show them this property without a pre-approval first, he sent them an exclusive buyer's agency agreement to sign. Jared signed it. He didn't quite understand what he signed. Now, it says right on there what it is, but he didn't really grasp what he was signing. Again, this is his first time buying a house. So, what Nick didn't do and what he should have done is he should have said, "Hey Jared, I understand that you're early on in the process. I understand that you don't have a pre-approval yet. I understand that you're not even ready to move. It's going to happen, you know, down the road. I'd be happy to go out and show you properties, but I need you to understand something. I need you to agree that I'm going to be your buyer's agent from here on out. So, if you decide over the next 6 months that you want to buy a house, you're committing to me to be your agent, which means any other properties that you go look at, I'm your agent, I need to work represent you, I need to help you go and purchase a property. Okay? And you're committed for 6 full months. And what that means, Jared, is if you buy another property without me being involved in it, I'm entitled to a commission anyways. So, I'm going to send this agreement to you, you're going to sign this agreement, and we're going to have this in place before I go and show you a property." It's what a good agent would have done. Helped a first-time home buyer understand how real estate agency works. He didn't do that. Jared signed the agreement. They went and looked at one property. That's it. Just one that one property. And then they don't talk again. 6 months goes by. Then this agent sees a YouTube video that I put out where I'm explaining how I'm helping Jared do his first deal. Jared found this property in Merriville, uh close by to where we live. I helped him through the process, but we contracted that property and we're supposed to close here in another week or so. And this agent saw that video, so he reaches out to Jared and he says, "Hey, you owe me a commission on that property you're buying because you signed a buyer's agent agreement and I'm supposed to be your agent and I'm supposed to get a commission. Okay?" And so, Jared tells me, "Dad, I got this text from this agent, Nick. What do I do?" And I said, "Well, hold on a minute. First of all, that was almost 6 months ago. That was for you to buy your primary residence as a first-time home buyer. He showed you one property. That was the end of it. You haven't communicated with this guy since. And now he thinks he's entitled to a commission on a property we're buying as an investment to flip that he had no part of. He was not part of that transaction whatsoever. And now he wants a 3% commission. By the way, it's a $115,000 property that we're buying. So, he's coming after a $3,000 commission that he feels like he's entitled to. So, I said, "First of all, that's got nothing to do with this. And second, we're buying the property in my LLC. I'm taking title. I'm owning this property. We're partnering, yes. But, I'm the one buying the property and I didn't sign a buyer's agreement with this guy." So, then Jared tells him that and he comes back and he says, "Well, your dad's dishonest because he's saying in the video that you're buying the property." Which I never said that. I said we're partnering and I'm helping him get his first deal. But, I'm the one buying the property. So, does he drop it? He does not drop it. He continues to pursue it. In fact, he threatens Jared that he's going to get legal involved and he's going to make sure that he gets his commission. And he goes even further than that and contacts the listing agent who we worked with to buy this investment property in Maryville. And so, that agent's calling us and like, "Who is this guy? Why's he contacting me? You know, is there an issue here with this guy?" So, he's just pursuing this even further. And he's doing all of this to try to get a $3,000 commission for work he did not do. Now, Nick, you've done a couple things here. You've alienated Jared. When he is ready to buy his first home, which he will be soon, he will not be contacting you and he will not be working with you. So, you alienated a first-time home buyer. You alienated me, which I'm an investor now looking to expand and grow. I plan on buying a lot of property in Knoxville. So, now you alienated me, which was a bad move. And you alienated the market because now here I am talking about it and sharing with other people how to avoid agents like you. All because you want a $3,000 check on work you did not do. Makes no sense to me why you would be pursuing this. Now, what is the takeaway here? What is the lesson that you can learn from this and how do you watch out for agents like this? Well, first of all, never sign exclusive buyers agency agreements. I just think there's no reason why you should sign one of those. So, first of all, let me make sure that I'm clear about this. I understand the reason for an exclusive buyer agency agreement. It's not fair to a buyer's agent to work with a buyer and go out and show them 10 properties, 15 properties, make offers, do all this work, and then have a buyer go around them and use a different agent and they get cut out. I get that. That's not what I'm talking about here, and that is not at all what happened here. This guy showed Jared one property while he was not approved to even buy a house, one property, and now he feels like he's entitled to this commission. So, that's why they have exclusive buyers agency agreement. So, what can you do instead of that? Why would you commit to that? Because here's the thing, you do not need a buyer's agent to show you property. You can find every property you could ever want on Zillow, Redfin, realtor.com online. So, buyers can go search for properties they're interested in, and now they do need to go see that property, but you don't need a buyer's agent to go see the property. Instead, contact the listing agent that has the listing on each and every property that you want to see. You call up the listing agent and you say, "Hey, I'm a buyer. I'm in the market. I'm interested in your listing. I'd like to go see it. If I end up making an offer on your listing, I'll let you do a specific buyer's agency agreement on your listing for just that offer. Meaning, if we don't get the deal, then I'm not locked into you to use you forever. Why would I commit 6 months or longer to a buyer's agent and I don't even know if they're any good just for them to go out and show me properties? And I don't need that. So, now if you want to see another property, you do the same thing. You contact that listing agent, and you say, "Hey, I'll let you represent me as the buyer. I'll gladly sign a buyer's agency agreement that's specific to just this property. And if we end up getting that, then you can actually dual represent. You can represent the the listing side, and you can represent the buyer side. You can get double commission, or we can negotiate the commission structure if you'd like, if you want to to help save on cost because you're getting both sides now, so you're making more money. That's called dual agency. Even in non-dual agency states, cuz there's a handful of states that don't do dual agency, even there you can what I call double dip, where you're getting both sides. That agent could be a transaction broker, where they don't represent either party, but they get both sides of the commission. Like that's Texas and Florida and some of the other states that don't have dual agency. So, my point here is work directly with a listing agent on their specific listing. Do a specific buyer's agency agreement just on their listings, and do that with each and every property that you want to see. It's a much better way to go, and you will avoid buyer's agents like this guy that you lock into and you're stuck with for 6 months. And guys like this guy, Nick, apparently will pursue it, even if they did nothing to earn it. This is a type of agent that you want to avoid. These are the type of agents that are, in my opinion, predatory. Like I said, should have never even had Jared sign that unless Jared understood the process, was pre-approved, and was ready to buy. I want to say this again. If you're a buyer, don't abuse an agent's time. That's not fair to the agent that you run them around and make them show you properties when you're not serious. So, be transparent as well. Just like the agent should be transparent with you about what they're doing, you need to be transparent with an agent and say, "Look, I've got my financing in place. I'm ready to buy. I want to go look at houses, and I'm going to commit, make an offer, and buy a house in the next 30 days, or whatever." In this case here, here's the big difference, and And why to me this is predatory. Nick is an agent that's active in the market. Like this is what he does. So he understands the process. Jared is the first time home buyer who does not understand the process. So who needs to be the responsible person in this transaction? The agent. The agent needs to be. He needs to explain to Jared, "Hey, here's what's going on here. Here's how this works. If you want me to show you a property, here's the commitment I want you to make to me. And here's what's going to happen if you break that commitment. Okay? We're going to sign a contract that I'm going to be holding you accountable to if you try to buy a property in the next 6 months. Like that would be the responsible thing to do. Explaining and being transparent is what it means to be a good agent or a good investor when you're dealing with people, especially the public who've never done it before. Guys, I have scripts with how I do all of my work with agents as an investor, what to say, how to say it, how to overcome objections, how to do the double dip, how to be transparent as an investor, a cash buyer, how to explain if you're wholesaling, all of the things that you need to do if you're working with an with an agent so that you're being transparent, you're disclosing, you're being honest, and you can build relationships with agents so that you can work together and get good good deals. Go to agentofferscripts.com to get the free download and I hope you find that you helpful and useful as you work with agents as an investor. And if you're a buyer, I hope you found this video helpful for what to watch out for and what to avoid when working with buyers agents. And I'll see you on the next video.

videos.transcript: So, when I think about a real estate transaction, there's really three people that have to be part of every single deal. There's the finder, which is going to be a wholesaler or an agent, there's the operator, that's the flipper or the buy and hold investor, and then you have the lender who's providing the capital. I think every real estate business, in the beginning, phase one of your business should be highly focused on acquisitions. And why do you think that is? videos.transcript: If you ever watch me call sellers live on YouTube, you'll see that I instantly know what price I need to be at when making offers. And these are properties that I'm just looking at for the first time. Now, if you plan on wholesaling virtually, where you offer, negotiate, and contract over the phone instead of in person at the property, then learning how to quickly and efficiently run the numbers is a skill you must learn and master. So, in this video, I'm going to show you exactly how I do it. Coming up. >> For a limited time, you can get a free copy of Jerry Norton's Offer Calculator, which gives you the offer price for any property in seconds. Download it now at freeoffercalculator.com. >> If you're new here, my name is Jerry Norton. I've been wholesaling and flipping real estate for over 20 years. And here on my YouTube channel, I show you how to master the process. So, if you want to be a flipping genius like me, subscribe to my channel and watch my videos. When it comes to wholesaling and flipping, I have two different business models. One is a backyard model, where we hyper-focus on a specific market, and we close deals on appointment at the properties. Now, in my backyard markets, the goal is to become what I call a local market expert and dominate that market and do seven figures plus annually. Now, the other model I do is a nationwide virtual business. This is where I buy nationwide leads, call sellers, offer, negotiate, and close over the phone without ever seeing the properties in person.
