videos.title: How to Tell Sellers You’re a Wholesaler (Without Killing the Deal)
videos.transcript: If you're going to wholesale residential real estate, it is critical you learn how to properly disclose to sellers that you are a wholesaler. As of this recording, there are at least 17 states with some form of wholesale regulation that requires disclosure, and my prediction is all states will eventually [music] make disclosure mandatory. The question is no longer, "Can I wholesale?" The question is, "What exact structure, disclosure, license, notice, timing, and marketing rules apply in >> [music] >> this state?" Wholesaling is now becoming state-specific. Not only do you need to learn the rules in whatever state you transact, you [music] also need to learn how to make disclosure a normal and natural part of your sale process. In this video, I'm going to explain why this is important and how to make it effortless as a wholesaler. All that and more coming up. >> [music] >> For a limited time, you can get a free copy of Jerry Norton's wholesaler contract pack with all the contracts you need to flip houses without [music] risk. Claim your free copy at wholesalercontracts.com. >> If you're new here, my name is Jerry Norton. I make millions of dollars a year wholesaling and flipping houses, and on this channel, I show you exactly how to do the same. So, if you want to be a flipping genius like me, subscribe to my channel and watch my videos. As the nation's leading expert on wholesaling, I've been tracking wholesale regulation since 2018. Across America, we're seeing more regulation and more disclosure requirements and more scrutiny of wholesaling activities. That's why I maintain a free report that outlines all of the different regulations state by state. To get the latest version for free, go to wholesalerregulations.com. I also maintain wholesale compliant contracts that I also give away for free. To get the latest version, go to wholesalercontracts.com. There are basically two types of wholesale regulation that many states have passed into law. The first is a licensing requirement. There are six or seven states that consider the act of wholesaling to be brokering and require an active real estate license in the state where you transact. These states include Delaware, Iowa, Pennsylvania, Illinois, Virginia, Alabama, and soon California. And there are also five or six states that consider publicly marketing a contract for sale to be brokering and require real estate license to do so. These states include Kentucky, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma, and Tennessee. Licensing regulation is usually headed up by the National Association of Realtors and falls under the jurisdiction of the state real estate commission. There isn't a whole lot you can do about that, but the second type of regulation is a direct result of consumer complaints from sellers who had a bad experience with a bad wholesaler. This regulation is all about disclosure. These laws are typically led by the state's consumer protection agency, and it's all about the seller being fully informed of what's going on. These states generally allow wholesaling, but require the wholesaler to disclose their role, equitable interest, intent to assign, profit potential, or seller cancellation rights. Examples include Arizona, Missouri, Ohio, Wisconsin, Maryland, Tennessee, Texas, Louisiana, and others. Some states allow the disclosure to be included in the purchase and sale agreement, and some states require a separate disclosure document. Again, all of this is outlined in my regulation report that you can download for free at wholesalerregulations.com. Disclosure in and of itself is pretty easy in my opinion. We'll talk more about what to say and how to do it in a minute, but the problem is some states are giving sellers more and more protection against wholesalers. Missouri, for example, requires a separate written disclosure at least 14 days before entering into the purchase and sale agreement. Delaware gives sellers a 21-day non-waivable cancellation right. Pennsylvania gives sellers a 30-day right to cancel. Think about it this way, licensing states regulate who can wholesale, disclosure states regulate how you wholesale. The point is, wherever you wholesale, whether it's your backyard, a remote market, or multiple markets, you need to understand the laws and follow them because the poor operators, even if unintentional, is what is causing more and stricter regulation. Everyone needs to learn how to operate with more honesty and more transparency. By the way, stay till the end of this video, I'm going to share a unique alternative method to wholesaling that does not apply to any wholesale regulations. But first, let's talk about how to disclose your wholesaler. First and foremost, let's get clear about your intent. Do you intend to assign your contract, or do you intend to buy the property? Lawmakers look at substance over form. Intent is defined by your transaction history and your ability to perform. In other words, if you have never purchased a property and you don't have the funds or the funding to purchase the property, then your intent was [clears throat] not to purchase the property. So, you can't say I'm a buyer if you can't show you've had a history of buying or if you don't have the means to buy. This matters because if you only have one option, assign the contract, then your disclosure and vernacular with sellers must be my intent is to assign the contract for a profit. If you do have a history or the means to buy, then you can say I may assign my contract for a profit. For example, I do both at a high level. I assign several contracts every month and I buy several properties every month. So, I can say to sellers with integrity, sometimes I buy directly and keep the property as a rental or a flip, and sometimes I assign my contract to other buyers. And I can stand behind that statement with a proven track record and a means to buy. Whereas, my good friend and pro wholesaler RJ Bates, he only assigns contracts. He doesn't buy and close on deals, so you won't ever hear him say, "I am going to buy your property." He will always say, "My goal is to sell the contract to an end buyer." This is important because if you misrepresent who you are in the transaction, you are inviting scrutiny from regulators. Now, whether your state requires disclosure and whether it's in your purchase and sale agreement or a separate document, let's talk about how to make disclosure a normal part of your sale process. The first step is to talk to the seller about the exit strategy in the third person. In other words, when talking about the property, refer to whatever the ideal end buyer would do. If the property is in a high rental market or the best exit strategy would be to hold the property for a rental, talk about what it would require to be a good rental. If the best exit strategy is to fix it and resell it, talk about what would need to happen for it to be a good fix and flip opportunity. So, rather than say, "I'm going to buy it to flip," say, "For this property to make sense to a flipper, I would need to fill in the blank." Another way to say this is, "If an investor were to buy this property, they would need a discount so they have room to fix it and flip it." Talking about the exit in the third person avoids misleading the seller that you are the end buyer. Step two is to negotiate a wholesale price just like you always do. Follow your normal analysis and sale process to get a discounted wholesale price. Step three is to explain to the seller that you intend to wholesale the property during your due diligence period. So, first let me explain how to do this if you sometimes buy and sometimes wholesale, and then I'll explain how to do this if you only wholesale. I'll say the following once I've got a commitment on price from the seller. "Mr. Seller, once we have a written agreement in place, I'll have a small window of due diligence, usually no more than 10 days. During that period, I'm going to need access to the property so that I can confirm my rehab budget. As long as everything checks out, we'll move forward to closing. If for some reason it doesn't, and our agreed-upon price doesn't work for me, then what I'll do is I'll reach out to all of the other active cash buyers in the area to see if they want to buy the property. If someone does, I'll assign the deal to them, and they'll step in and buy the property directly from you. Now, don't worry, they'll pay me a fee, so it won't cost you anything, and it won't come out of the agreed-upon price. So, either way, I'm going to go to work very hard to get you a buyer for your property. That's my commitment to you. If for some reason I can't buy it, and none of the local active buyers want it, I'll let you know right away, and we can revisit what to do at that point. Does that sound fair? Do you have any questions about what happens next? Now, do you see how I explained that? It's not difficult. I've never explained it that way and had a seller not want to move forward. Now, I believe proper disclosure, explained the right way, actually helps your sales process because it sets the seller up for a possible renegotiation later if needed, so they're not offended by that. So, what does this look like if you wholesale only? Well, here's how to say it. Mr. Seller, once we have an agreement in place, let me explain what happens next. In our agreement, I'll have a due diligence window, usually no more than 10 days. During that period, I'm going to need access to the property. The reason is I work with a large network of local active cash buyers and investors in the area. These are my partners, in effect, and my job is to identify which of them would be the best fit for this property. Once I find the right partner, I'll assign the deal to them, and they'll step in and fund the purchase on the day of closing. But, don't worry, they pay me a fee for bringing the deal, so you still get the agreed-upon price. If for some reason none of my partners want the deal, I'll let you know right away, and we can decide together what to do from there. Does that make sense? Do you have any questions? Now, even if disclosure wasn't required by law, isn't explaining to the seller the wholesaling process better than the seller being confused as to what is happening and finding out later? I'm convinced that if you explain it up front, you avoid all kinds of problems later. Now, if your state does have mandated disclosures, then you also want to verbally discuss the written disclosures and the seller rights. Don't pretend like it's not there or gloss over it. Tackle it head-on. Say to the sellers, "This section in our agreement talks about my intent to assign the contract for a profit. Let's review this part so I can answer any questions you may have." Like all communications, it's always better to talk about things up front than to have them come up later when there's confusion and a seller's angry because he didn't understand what was happening. Now, let's talk about timing. Disclosure is not just about what to say, it's also about when you say it. Some states require disclosure before the contract execution, at contract execution, before assignment, several days before assignment, or several days before even signing the purchase agreement. Missouri, for example, requires a standalone disclosure at least 14 days before the purchase agreement. Tennessee requires a 3-day notice to the seller before contracting with a new buyer. The point is a correct disclosure given at the wrong time may still be non-compliant. If your state doesn't have a specific timing requirement, here's how I recommend you handle it. If you're closing on the phone, you could disclose wholesaling after getting a verbal commitment on price but before you send the contract to be signed. In that case, say to a seller, "Give me about 5 minutes to get the agreement over to your inbox, but let me explain what happens next." Then I'll talk about my intent to wholesale. Or you could wait until the seller has the agreement in front of them and then you review it together and discuss disclosure. And if the seller just signs your contract without even reading it, which happens all the time, then disclose wholesaling after he signs the agreement. Sometimes I'll wait until after I send a runner to the property to get pictures and video and I know what I'm dealing with. The point is if not mandated by law, whether it's before, during, or after the signing, always explain and disclose the wholesale process before you start doing dispo. Do not send buyers to the property or attempt to assign your contract without the seller being fully informed as to what's happening. Lawmakers want sellers to be fully educated on what is happening, what their options are, and what their rights are, and it's better that way anyways. So, I want you right now to leave a comment and say, "I get it, Jerry. Always disclose wholesaling to a seller according to the law and before starting the dispo process." Now, throw in there, "You're a flipping genius." for good measure. And I also want to take a minute and give a word of caution. Do not cloud title as leverage. Recording memorandums, affidavits, liens, or other documents to pressure a seller is becoming a major target. Louisiana and Oklahoma passed laws that prohibit recording encumbrances to force seller performance or prevent the seller from accepting another offer. Connecticut also restricts recorded documents intended to cloud title or prevent a transfer. Using title as a weapon is one of the fastest ways to attract regulatory trouble. Regarding regulation, the bottom line is this. The wholesalers who survived 2026 and beyond will be the ones who understand that compliance, including disclosure, is now part of the business model. You need better disclosures, better contracts, better marketing language, better records, and better state-by-state procedures. The opportunity is still massive in wholesale real estate, but you have to learn how to do it the right way. So, what happens when regulation makes traditional wholesaling illegal like South Carolina or too difficult to be worth it like Pennsylvania, Delaware, or Missouri? One of the strategies I'm implementing more and more is what I call the takedown method. This is where you contract a discounted property for sale just like before, but rather than wholesaling the deal, you actually buy the property and take title with no predetermined buyer. By doing so, you are not transferring contractual rights. You are indeed the end buyer. So, wholesale disclosure, licensing, or any other wholesale regulation doesn't apply. Once you fund and close the deal, you immediately list the property for sale on the MLS without rehabbing it and resell it on the open market for a profit. And here's the best part. Using the takedown method, we typically make two to four times more on a deal than traditional wholesaling without rehabbing. So, if you'd like to learn exactly how I analyze, fund, and sell deals using the takedown method, I put together a free takedown kit. Inside, you'll get my deal analyzer, my seller scripts, my funding pitch deck, and the exact framework I use to structure these deals. Just go to freetakedownkit.com. In fact, watch this next video where I explain [music] 10 threats facing wholesalers in 2026 and why most won't survive. You'll [music] learn what you need to do to not just survive, but thrive as a wholesaler. Watch that now and I'll see you [music] on the next video.

videos.title: Forget Houses… Flipping Land Is Easier
videos.transcript: Most real estate investors are obsessed with houses and don't get me wrong, I love houses, too, but there's another type of real estate that most investors completely ignore, vacant land. Here's the crazy part, in many cases, land is actually easier to flip than houses. There's no roof [music] inspections, no foundation issues, no rehab budgets, no contractors, no $40,000 surprise hiding behind the drywall. It's just [music] dirt. And although land is not sexy, it can be extremely profitable. So, in this video, I'm going to break down seven different ways you can profit flipping land, and I'll even show you exactly how to get your next land deal in as little as 30 days. All that and more coming up. >> For a limited time, you can get a free copy of Jerry Norton's vacant lot finder software, which finds empty lots that you can flip for profit. [music] Get it now at vacantlotfinder.com. >> If you're new here, my name is Jerry Norton. I make millions of dollars a year wholesaling and flipping real estate, and on this channel, I show you exactly how to do the same. So, if you want to be a flipping genius like me, subscribe to my channel and watch my videos. The first method to flip land is the most common, and that is infill lot flipping. An infill lot is a vacant lot inside an existing subdivision, neighborhood, or city. Picture a street with 30 houses on it, and right in the middle of that street is one empty lot. That's an infill lot. And these vacant infill lots can be extremely valuable to a spec builder, which is someone who builds and flips new construction houses. The strategy is to buy a buildable lot, build a new construction home that meets the demands of the market, and then flip it to a retail buyer for top dollar. In fact, this is one of my primary flipping strategies. Over the years, I've built and flipped hundreds of new construction homes. As a flipper, I love new construction because it's less competitive than rehabbing. It's easier than rehabbing because everything is brand new and there aren't any unforeseen surprises and retail buyers typically pay as much as 20% more for a new home over an existing home. I think the reason is in most markets there is a shortage of new housing and investors like me who specialize in flipping new construction are eagerly looking for buildable lots. In fact, I have systems and capital in place to build and flip new homes in any market in the US and I'm always looking for good buildable lots where I can build and flip new construction. Now if you'd like to learn how you can get paid to bring me buildable lots that meet my criteria, then I want to invite you to a free training where you can learn how to become a lot finder for me. I'll put the link to register for that free training in the description below. And be sure to stay to the end of this video. I'm going to share with you a free tool that will help you find your next buildable lot in as little as 30 days. Okay, sometimes with infill lots it's just a vacant lot sitting in a desirable area and sometimes there's an old house where there's more value in the lot. When that happens the new construction flipper will tear down the old house and build a new one. Let me give you an example. While doing live seller calls on YouTube, I talked to a seller who owned an uninhabitable teardown house in a high-end neighborhood in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. She agreed to sell the property to me but the value was not in the house but in the land. Two doors down there was a new construction home actively listed for sale. So once I had this infill lot under contract, I called the spec builder and sure enough he was very interested in my infill lot. So I ended up wholesaling it to him for a $20,000 wholesale fee. Now what was nice about that deal was there was no rehab to figure out. I just matched an undervalued piece of land with a builder who already knows what to do with it. Okay, the second method to flip land is what I call micro land banking. Now, this is when you're looking for vacant lots in areas that are starting to improve but are not fully redeveloped yet. Maybe the area is still a little rough. Maybe values haven't exploded yet. But, you can see signs of change. New stores are popping up, old buildings are getting remodeled, investors are starting to buy, new construction is popping up nearby, a major retailer or development is coming down the road. This is not necessarily land that you sell to a builder tomorrow. This is land you sell to a financial buyer. This is a buyer who takes money out of the stock market or other investments and parks it in land for the next 5, 10, or 15 years. They're betting that the area will improve and the land will appreciate. That's land banking. But, instead of buying hundreds of acres, this is micro land banking, one lot at a time. The opportunity is not to hold it and become a land banker. You can do that if you want, but the opportunity is to flip to someone else who wants to hold it. Your profit is not holding on for 10 years. Your profit is holding on for 10 minutes. That's the flipper mindset. You find the deal and you sell it to that person that wants to hold on to it. Your buyer is usually an investor who believes in the future of that area and wants to park money in land before values increase. Okay, the third method is what I call path of growth land. Now, this is land outside the city but in the direction the city is growing. It may be 10 miles out. It might be 20 miles out. It might be 30 miles out. But, the key question is, where is the growth headed? Are subdivisions moving that direction? Are roads being expanded? Are utilities moving that way? Are builders buying nearby? Are major employers, schools, hospitals, or retail developments moving in that corridor? That path of growth land can be attractive even if the big appreciation is 10 or 15 years away because buyers are thinking ahead. I'll give you an example of this. I live in East Tennessee and the other day I was talking to a real estate agent who represents the Clayton family who owns Clayton Homes, and they're heavily investing in a town called Townsend. You find a 2-acre, 5-acre, or 10-acre parcel outside a growing city. The owner has no plans for it. They bought it years ago, inherited it, or just don't care about it anymore. You get it under contract at a discount, then you sell it to someone who wants land in that path of growth. Like I said, this could be a retiree, it could be a land banker, a small builder, a family that wants space, or an investor betting on growth. The fourth method is what I call mini ranch flipping. Now, this one is especially interesting because the buyer pool is emotional. These are usually larger rural parcels, 10 acres, 20 acres, 40 acres, sometimes more. This is the RV, ATV, dirt bike, shooting, camping, weekend getaway crowd. These are people with trucks, trailers, Razors, dirt bikes, campers, hunting gear, and outdoor toys. Now, let's discuss some additional land flipping strategies that may require investment capital. So, the fifth method is seller-financed land flipping. Now, this is where you get a land deal at a discount, but instead of wholesaling it, you buy it and then resell it using seller-financed terms. Here's an example. You buy a piece of land for, let's say, $10,000. You turn around and resell it for $25,000 with seller financing. The buyer gives you $2,500 down and pays you $400 a month. Seller financing is actually very common with land because it's typically harder to get traditional financing on vacant land, so land owners are much more willing. Now, following this method, you turned a land deal into monthly cash flow. And depending on your numbers, you may get most or all of your original investment back from the down payment, then collect payments over time. The cash flip gives you fast money, but the seller finance flip gives you long-term income. Both can work, it just depends on your goals. Method six is what I call the subdividing land flipping method. This is where you buy a tract of land and you get it re-zoned into smaller parcels, then sell off the parcels individually. Now, I'm doing a deal right now just like this. I bought 57 acres that I'm having split into five different lots. Doing so, I can literally double my money. Usually, there's time involved to get re-zoning and also cost for appraisals, surveys, perk tests, and so on, but subdividing can be very profitable. Method seven is what I call value-add land flipping. This is where you buy vacant land and prove it in some way or another, then sell it for a profit. I'll give another example of a smaller project I'm doing right now. I recently bought three RV lots in a mobile home park in Sanibel Island, Florida. videos.title: Missouri Just Changed Wholesaling Forever! (NEW LAW)
videos.transcript: Missouri wholesalers, you need to hear this. Starting October 28th, you no longer are able to sign a contract with a motivated seller the same day you meet them. Instead, Missouri's new law forces you to wait 14 days before you can even put a property under contract. That's a massive [music] change and it's going to drastically change the way we wholesale in Missouri. And if you don't understand these new rules, you could lose deals, lose earnest [music] money, and be subject to fines and penalties. In this video, I'm going to explain exactly [music] what this law is and what you need to do to stay compliant. Coming up. >> For a limited time, you can get a free copy of Jerry Norton's wholesaler contract pack with all the contracts you [music] need to flip houses without risk. Claim your free copy at wholesalercontracts.com. >> This isn't the first time Missouri lawmakers have tried to regulate wholesaling. Concerns around wholesalers have been building for years as consumer complaints increased. But unlike previous discussions and proposals, this time lawmakers actually got a bill across the finish line and it fundamentally changes how wholesalers will operate in Missouri going forward. What's important here is that Missouri isn't alone. We're seeing a clear national trend. States across the country are taking a closer look at wholesaling and Missouri is just the latest state to enact significant new disclosure requirements. As the nation's leading expert on wholesaling, I've been tracking wholesale regulations since 2018. Be sure to get the latest report which outlines all of the different regulations state by state including this new law in Missouri. To download my free nationwide wholesale regulation report, go to wholesaleregulations.com. I also maintain wholesale compliant contracts that I also give away for free. To get the latest version, go to wholesalercontracts.com. Okay, now let's get into it. Missouri legislators passed Senate Bill 973 which creates new disclosure requirements for real estate wholesalers operating on residential one-to-four unit properties. The bill has been delivered to the governor and once he signs, it becomes effective August 28th, 2026. Now, before anybody freaks out, wholesaling is not illegal in Missouri. Let me repeat that. Wholesaling is still legal, but the process is changing dramatically. Here's the bombshell. The law requires wholesalers to provide a written disclosure to the seller at least 14 calendar days before entering into a purchase contract. The disclosure must be a separate standalone document signed by both parties. Now, think about that. Most wholesalers today operate like this. Lead comes in, you call the seller, you either negotiate and sign a contract on the phone, or you set an appointment, meet the seller, and sign a contract at the kitchen table. Either way, the goal is to execute a contract as soon as possible. There is a saying in wholesale real estate that I've been teaching for years. Time kills all deals. The longer you wait, the higher likelihood that you lose the deal. In Missouri, things just got more complicated. Let's say that you meet a seller on September 1st. Under the new law, you would provide the disclosure on September 1st. Then, you would wait September 2nd, September 3rd, September 10th, September 14th, and the earliest you could potentially sign the purchase agreement would be September 15th. Now, that completely changes the acquisition process. You may be wondering, "Why did Missouri do this?" Well, like I've been saying for years, you brought it upon yourself. According to supporters of the bill, lawmakers were responding to consumer complaints involving wholesalers. Issues cited included sellers not understanding assignments, investors clouding title with equitable interest filings, sellers not realizing contracts could be assigned for profit, homeowners feeling pressured into agreements they didn't fully understand. All of these issues could have easily been avoided if our industry could learn how to operate with integrity and transparency. And honestly, as professional investors, transparency should already be part of our business. Now, I've always believed sellers should understand exactly who they're dealing with and exactly how the transaction works. All I can say is it's your own fault. Is 14 days excessive? Yes, but here we are. So, what exactly must be disclosed? Well, the seller must receive a separate written disclosure explaining things like you are acting as a wholesaler, you may assign or transfer the contract, you may profit from the transfer, you may never actually take title, and the property may ultimately be sold for more money than what the wholesaler agreed to accept. Again, this disclosure cannot simply be buried inside a purchase agreement. It must be a standalone document. That's why I've already updated my free contract pack with a Missouri specific writer and standalone disclosure form. You can grab it free at wholesalercontracts.com. So, what happens if you don't comply, which undoubtedly will happen because for some reason most wholesalers don't bother to learn the laws and the rules where they transact or just don't care. But, non-compliance is a big deal. If a wholesaler fails to provide the required disclosure, the seller can cancel the transaction prior to closing. That's a huge risk. The seller is also entitled to keep the wholesaler's earnest money deposit, and violations fall under Missouri consumer protection laws, which could expose wholesalers to investigations by the attorney general, civil lawsuits, restitution, loss of profits, attorney's fees, and other penalties. In other words, this is not something that you want to ignore. >> Still paying [music] for property data? PropStream gives you unlimited property data, comps, and more for free. Download the PropStream [music] app on the App Store or Google Play Store today. >> Now, the real question you should be asking is what can you and can't you do? In other words, what exactly constitutes wholesaling? Well, the statute defines a wholesaler as someone who enters into a purchase contract as a grantee to acquire an interest in residential real property from a record owner and seeks to sell or assign the wholesaler's interest for a profit. In plain English, if you contract with a seller and then you intend to transfer your contractual rights to another buyer for a fee, you're operating as a wholesaler under this law. Now, that clearly includes traditional assignments. Novations are covered as well because you're still transferring or substituting contractual rights for a profit. In both those situations, the investor never actually takes title to the property. Now, you may be wondering what about back-to-back double closings? That's the million-dollar question and the answer isn't entirely clear. The honest answer is nobody knows for certain yet. Here's why. You put the property under contract and then you assign your contractual rights to another buyer. But in a true back-to-back double closing, you're doing something very different. You actually close on the property, you take legal title, even if only for a minute, and then you sell the real estate that you own. You're not assigning your contract, you're selling a property. And because of that distinction, many investors and attorneys believe that a true double closing likely falls outside the scope of the statute. However, and this is important, Missouri lawmakers could argue that if the primary purpose of the transaction is still to profit from acquiring and immediately reselling distressed residential real estate, the law could apply. At this point, there is no case law, no regulatory guidance, and no official interpretation answering that question. So, here's my recommendation. If you're assigning or innovating contracts in Missouri, assume this law absolutely applies. If you're doing true back-to-back double closings, consult a competent Missouri legal counsel and make sure that your specific process is compliant. Personally, if I were doing double closings in Missouri after August 28th, I would want a Missouri attorney to review my exact closing process before proceeding. As more guidance becomes available, I'll definitely keep you updated. But, here's the bigger takeaway. Missouri isn't the first state to regulate wholesaling, and it won't be the last. Across America, we're seeing more regulation, more disclosure requirements, and more scrutiny of wholesaling activities. The professional wholesalers are going to adapt. Amateurs are going to disappear. The investors who survive will be the ones who understand compliance, operate transparently, and run a real business. So, be sure to stay compliant. Again, download my free nationwide wholesale regulation report along with my free wholesale contract pack that now includes the Missouri writer and standalone disclosure forms. This is where you contract a discounted property just like you did before, but rather than assigning, innovating, or double closing, you actually buy the property and take title with no predetermined buyer. By doing so, you are not transferring contractual rights. You are indeed the end buyer, so wholesale disclosure, licensing, or any other wholesale regulation doesn't apply. Once you fund and close the deal, you immediately list the property for sale on the MLS without rehabbing it, and you resell it on the open market for a profit. Now here's the best part, using the takedown method we typically make two to four times more on deals than traditional wholesaling without rehabbing. Inside you'll get my deal analyzer, seller scripts, a funding pitch deck, and the exact framework I use to structure deals. Just go to freetakedownkit.com. In fact, let me show you a recent deal that I couldn't wholesale because there were no buyers, but following [music] the takedown method I made a $10,000 profit. So watch that now and I'll see you [music] on the next video.

videos.title: Virtual Wholesaling Is Broken... Here's Why
videos.transcript: Virtual wholesaling can be a beautiful thing when everything goes well, but when it doesn't, it can result in a lot of wasted time and potentially be harmful to sellers. On this video, I'm going to share the biggest mistakes virtual wholesalers make and how to fix them. Now, if you implement these changes, you'll improve your close ratio by 46%. Coming up. >> For a limited time, you can get a free copy of Jerry Norton's [music] virtual wholesaling guide so you can flip houses online without leaving your home. >> [music] >> Download it now at virtualwholesaleguide.com. >> The challenge with virtual wholesaling is you're closing a seller on the phone without first having seen the property or the neighborhood and often times in a market you don't understand or have any previous experience with. Now, if you don't know, here's how virtual wholesaling works. You talk to a seller who expressed an interest in selling his property. You ask questions to uncover motivation, find out if there's urgency, and to understand the condition. Then, without first seeing the property, you make an educated decision on the value, run a buy formula, and then verbally negotiate what you believe is a profitable wholesale price. Once in agreement, you send a digital contract to the seller's email, and once he signs, you now have an executed contract on a property you've never seen before. And like I said, when done properly and everything works out, it's awesome. In fact, I often call sellers live on YouTube and I show how to wholesale virtually. I'm going to put below a link to a video where I called a seller live, I locked up the deal on the spot, and it resulted in a $20,000 wholesale profit. I mean, let's be honest, there is nothing better than sitting in your air-conditioned home office in your underwear making millions of dollars wholesaling houses. That's the dream right there. However, when it doesn't work out and you later discover that you overcontracted, and you spent a lot of time, energy, and effort just to end up canceling the contract, that's frustrating and demoralizing, not to mention potentially harmful to the seller. And that's the reality. Most virtual wholesalers have a high contract fallout rate, which no doubt is contributing to more and stricter regulations. Now, to prove my point, I recently saw a post on Facebook from a virtual wholesaler who said he's contracted 27 properties since he started and only closed four of them. That's a 15% close rate, which is really low. But even successful virtual wholesalers have to terminate a lot of contracts. I have a virtual wholesaler that does seven figures annually, and he told me he only closes 50% of contracts. That means half of all contracts never make it to the closing table. That is a lot of wasted time, energy, and resources. Now, to be fair, in wholesaling, we're dealing with distressed properties, which also means it's common to have issues with title, but even still, in my backyard market, where we meet sellers in person before signing contracts, we have an 80% close ratio, and that 20% that doesn't close is mostly from title issues out of our control, not from overcontracting. So, why do virtual wholesalers have such a low close rate, and what can be done to improve it? In my experience, the first and biggest reason is the properties are too rural. My definition of rural is any location that is more than an hour drive from a metro market. Now, super rural is 2 hours from a metro, and super duper rural is 3 hours from a metro. You get the point. Why do wholesalers chase rural deals? The answer is simple. Rural leads are cheap. Let's take a paper lead provider like Lead Zolo. In a major metro market, you could pay 400 or more for one exclusive lead, whereas in a rural location that same exclusive lead might only be $50 or less. So, in an effort to spend less on marketing, virtual wholesalers buy the cheap rural leads only to shoot themselves in the foot with low conversions. It's easy to acquire a rural property at a discount. The problem is they are difficult to dispo due to a lack of cash buyers. Now, in my experience, here's what I found. The metro cash buyers will often go about an hour away for a deal, but any further and it gets more difficult. The biggest lesson is this, the fewer the cash buyers, the harder to wholesale, which means the more rural the property, the more difficult to find a cash buyer. So, my first recommendation is to avoid rural. Spend the extra money and buy leads in better locations. You think you're saving money, but the truth is you'll close more deals and for higher fees if you buy higher quality leads. Now, if you're budget conscious, then buy leads on the fringe, right at that hour away from a metro location. >> Find deals faster with Propwire. Search properties, >> [music] >> skip trace owners, and get lead alerts. Download the Propwire app on the App Store or Google Play Store for free. >> That way you can still attract the metro buyers. Now, if you do buy rural leads, then I have two more suggestions. Contract that deal so dirt cheap that you can't lose. I'm talking about 10% of its current value. It better be so discounted that one of the 14 buyers in town won't be able to say no. My second recommendation is to do what I often do, and that is to take it down and buy it. I call that the takedown method. Get it? Take it down. The strategy here is to close on it and immediately relist it on the open market, no rehabbing. The idea is that once it's on the open market, you'll find that one cash buyer hiding under a rock. Now, I just did this on a rural deal in Galax, Virginia. I bought the worst house ever for $3,500 and I resold it for $10,000. I also did this on a house in Vidor, Texas. I bought it for 34,000 and I resold it for 52,500. Now, if you want to learn more how to do the takedown method, I have an entire training with resources that I'll give to you for free. Just go to freetakedownkit.com to get that download. Now, the second reason virtual wholesalers have a high cancel rate is because they don't set up proper expectations with the seller for a potential renegotiation. You see, the mistake most virtual wholesalers make is they over-convey certainty to the seller. In an effort to win the deal, they lead the seller to believe that their offer is solid and firm. So, the seller banks on your ability to perform, and then when you can't, they are offended and upset, killing any chances of restructuring the deal. I can't tell you how many deals I do where I'm cleaning up a mess from a previous wholesaler where the seller had a really negative experience with that wholesaler who didn't perform. Look, creating certainty with a seller is a powerful close technique if you're in person when you see the house and the neighborhood and you have confidence in your numbers. But with virtual, it's a double-edged sword that often backfires. The better strategy that will actually create more goodwill is to convey to the seller that you have a lack of certainty in your ability to perform, which is actually more honest. Now, I believe this one modification in your sales process will set you up properly for a renegotiation if and when you find yourself over-contracted. Let me show you what this looks like. I'll give an example that just happened while calling sellers live on YouTube with my friend and pro wholesaler RJ Bates. After talking to the seller for 15 or 20 minutes, I negotiated what I thought was a good deal. I said to the seller, "Mr. Seller, I understand 95,000 is your absolute bottom line, and I think that's a fair price, but it's not quite where I need to be. If it was 75,000, I would be much more confident. However, I'm really connected with a lot of active cash buyer investors. If you will give me a window of time, I will work really hard to find you a buyer willing to pay 95,000. And don't worry, they'll pay me out of the deal, so you still get the 95,000 at closing. I only need about 10 days to work my network. I can't promise you I can get the deal done for 95, but I can promise you I'll work really hard. If after the 10 days I can't secure a buyer, we can revisit the deal and decide what to do from there." Now, Mr. Seller, I will need you to commit to me with an agreement because I can't spend the time on it and then you sell to someone else. Does that seem like a fair arrangement? Now, what just happened? I just explained wholesaling, and I prepped the seller for a potential renegotiation. Now, there's no guarantee you don't waste your time and can't find a buyer, so make sure you actually think 95,000 is a deal, but at least he's not offended later when you can't perform because you explained clearly the process and what happens if you can't find a buyer. So, let's say in that example, your highest offer you get from a cash buyer is 95,000. Now, you go back to the seller and you renegotiate to 85,000 or whatever you want. There's no guarantee the seller will lower the price, but because you set up proper expectations, your chances are greatly increased because you were honest and transparent. Now, be sure to structure correctly and execute a contract and assign it to your buyer and follow all the state required regulations, but following this technique, you'll get way more deals across the finish line, and you'll increase your close ratio by a whopping 46%. I just made that but it will go up a lot. And I can't reiterate this enough. Do not spend time working on a deal that you don't have under contract. Explain to the seller the next steps. Mr. Seller, I'm going to email you an agreement to approve. I cannot start working on this until you have that in place. Once we do, I'll send someone out to do a walk-through, and we'll get pictures and video, and then I'll get to work with my buyers. But like I said, if I can't make 95,000 work, we'll revisit this, and we'll come up with a new plan. If we do decide to move forward after the 10 days, I'll open escrow, I'll put down earnest money, and we'll close on the agreed-upon date. Now, one more tip. Never renegotiate a seller without having your buyer locked in. You get one shot to renegotiate a seller, so don't blow it. Get the buyer to commit. I'll say to the buyer, "If I can get you this deal at 95,000, are you willing to commit in writing and put down non-refundable earnest money?" If they are unwilling, you don't have a serious buyer. So, if you found this video helpful, leave a comment and say, "Thank you, Jerry. You are a flipping genius." And if you're new to virtual wholesaling, be sure to get my free virtual wholesaling kit with all of the resources you need to get your first virtual deal in the next 30 days. Now, for that free download, just go to virtualwholesaleguide.com. Finally, watch this next video where I show a case study on how I had a $20,000 profit [music] doing a virtual wholesale deal. Watch that now, and I'll see you on the [music] next video.
